name: NIAR Additive Manufacturing Techno-Economic Analysis cost model and TEA module (America Makes IMPACT project 5554.007)
year: 2023–2025 (period of performance Nov 14, 2023 to May 14, 2025; no final deliverable found publicly as of Oct 2026)
developer: Wichita State University National Institute for Aviation Research (NIAR), VALDOS group (team listed in the briefing: Brady Williams, R. Andrulonis, M. Shaw, L. Tubesing, C. Combemale, P. Funk; no PI is labeled). Funded by OSD ManTech through AFRL agreement FA8650-20-2-5700 and administered by America Makes (project 5554.007; IMPACT Topic 8, Project 2).
description: A cost model for four metal AM modalities, plus a techno-economic analysis (TEA) module 'to be used by DoD personnel to aid in the decision of when to leverage AM'. The stated objective is to 'deliver a framework for when, where, and how to utilize metal AM technologies to bridge gaps in component sourcing.' The team compared 13 existing cost models and used advisory-board and government interviews to find omitted cost elements; the stated future work is to 'implement the gaps into a tool.' This update re-read the Jan 2024 interim briefing and searched for other NIAR tools built for the Air Force. None were found. NIAR's other Air Force work is B-1/F-16 digital twins, WAM materials data and scanning/reverse engineering. The ratings describe the planned cost structure in the interim briefing, not a verified final tool.
NRE_note: The interim briefing lists 'NRE (DFAM, engineering salary, etc.)' only as an item in an 'Initial Gap Analysis for LPBF Cost Model' (slide 13), and CAD/DFAM/machine-setup rows appear in a literature-review table of cost elements by modality. The NIAR/TEA model is a planned deliverable with no values, formulas or calculations published.
Production_note: Per-modality cost elements (feedstock, build plate, machine cost, depreciation, labor, energy, gas, build time, post-processing) are listed from a review of 13 existing cost models. NIAR's own model is planned ('implementation of gaps into deliverable tool'), and no calculation or values are public.
QA_Qual_note: Appears only as 'supplier learning curve/common qualification', an industry-maturation factor. There is no qualification-campaign cost element (interim briefing).
QA_Insp_note: 'Quality Control' appears as a row in the literature-review cost-element table, and 'inspection rate per part application' appears as a gap item for a planned LPBF model. No inspection-cost method or values are public.
Storage_note: The advisory board flagged 'Packaging and storage' as an element missing from traditional cost models, to be added in the TEA module. It is not shown as quantified.
Shared_Capital_note: Machine depreciation, wrap rates and the build-plate packing factor spread capital within builds. No sharing across a part portfolio or across users is shown.
Shared_Capacity_note: The interim briefing's objective says 'when, where, and how' but has no site, location, capacity or utilization content, and the final tool is not public.
Speed_note: 'Readiness/AOG', 'costs associated with inoperable equipment and/or vehicles' and 'supply chain alleviation' are listed as TEA factors to add. Lead time is not modeled in the briefing.

name: DLA Legacy Parts AM Prescreening Tool (DLA prototype AM candidate selection tool)
developer: LMI with XSB Inc., Penn State (T. Simpson) and Virginia Tech (C. Williams), for the Defense Logistics Agency Weapon System Sustainment Program
description: A database query tool that narrows about 4.5 million DLA-managed parts to about 43,000 that fit an AM build envelope and exactly match a common AM feedstock, assuming no redesign. Users then filter by FSC, weapon system, criticality, lead time, unit cost, dimensions, material and machine, with engineering review of each candidate's technical data package (TDP) required before any decision.
NRE_note: TDP availability is a displayed attribute, a proxy for reverse-engineering need; NRE is not costed and no redesign is assumed.
Production_note: Unit cost (current price) is a filter; no AM production cost is computed.

Storage_note: Annual demand and backorder status are proposed data elements; stock on hand is only a consideration. No inventory or holding-cost analysis.
Shared_Capital_note: Not addressed.
Shared_Capacity_note: Not addressed.
Speed_note: Combined administrative plus production lead time and backorder data are filters; not converted to readiness value.

name: NAVSEA AM part risk triage and TDP approval framework (with NAMPIE part identification events)

NRE_note: The AM page does not mention setup or engineering charges, and no product documentation was read.
Production_note: Automated pricing from support volume, material volume, orientation and runtime (Paperless Parts AM page).
QA_Qual_note: The AM page does not mention qualification, and no product documentation was read.
QA_Insp_note: The AM page does not mention inspection, which job-shop quotes can include as a line item.
Storage_note: Paperless Parts prices jobs for a manufacturer, so inventory holding is outside its documented scope.
Shared_Capital_note: Estimates number of parts per build; machine amortization not shown (Paperless Parts AM page).
Shared_Capacity_note: Paperless Parts prices jobs for one shop and does not address capacity shared across sites or users.
Speed_note: The AM page mentions fast turnaround but does not say whether lead times are quoted.

name: DigiFabster (AM quoting and e-commerce)
year: Unknown (active by Nov 2021; integrated with Materialise CO-AM Nov 2023)
developer: DigiFabster (US-based)
description: ML-assisted instant quoting and e-commerce for AM service providers, using one-off per-build costs (e.g., recoat time driven by part height in powder bed) and per-part material and machine time; order data flows into Materialise CO-AM.
NRE_note: DigiFabster's cost-based pricing includes setup and programming costs as one-off charges (Instant Quoting page, 2026), but design, digitization and parameter development are not covered.
Production_note: Quote logic uses per-part material consumption and production time plus one-off costs (3DPI DigiFabster guest post 2021).
QA_Qual_note: The quoting pages and the 2021 guest post do not mention qualification, and no product documentation was read.
QA_Insp_note: The pages do not mention inspection, but pricing parameters are user-configurable, so an inspection charge cannot be ruled out.
Storage_note: DigiFabster is a job quoting and ordering tool for manufacturers, so inventory holding is outside its documented scope.
Shared_Capital_note: Recognizes shared build costs (powder-bed recoat time shared by parts on a build); amortization not shown (3DPI 2021).
Shared_Capacity_note: DigiFabster prices jobs for one shop and does not address capacity shared across sites or users.
Speed_note: The quoting pages and the 2021 guest post do not say whether lead times are quoted.

name: Rickenbacher integrated SLM cost model
developer: L. Rickenbacher, A. Spierings, K. Wegener (ETH Zurich / inspire AG)
description: Adapts Alexander et al.'s generic cost model to SLM, covering pre- and post-processing steps plus a regression-based build-time estimate for mixed build jobs. It allocates build cost to parts by volume and build height so that parts of different size and complexity sharing one build each get a fair cost. Building parts simultaneously gave a 41% average cost reduction in the case study.
NRE_note: Geometry-data preparation and build-job assembly are cost elements (per Dogea et al. 2023's description of the model). These are recurring build prep, with no redesign, reverse engineering or parameter development.
Production_note: Core output is total cost per part for parts of differing size, complexity and quantity; each process step is modelled (Emerald abstract).
QA_Qual_note: Only the abstract and two secondary descriptions were read; Dogea et al. (2023) say nothing about quality or qualification, so whether the model includes them is not established.
QA_Insp_note: The abstract says the model covers all pre- and post-processing steps, but neither it nor the secondary descriptions say whether inspection is one of them (only heat treatment and HIP are confirmed absent).
Storage_note: Outside the documented scope: the model allocates SLM process-step costs to parts in shared build jobs, which does not involve inventory (Emerald abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: Explicitly models simultaneous builds of multiple parts from different projects, with cost-allocation algorithms; 41% average per-part reduction (abstract). Rudolph & Emmelmann 2018 describe the split by volume and build height.
Shared_Capacity_note: Pooling happens only within one machine's build jobs, as a cost effect; no lead-time or multi-site capacity effect.
Speed_note: Not addressed.

name: Lindemann et al. (2013) DMRC lifecycle-cost model with TD-ABC
developer: C. Lindemann, U. Jahnke, M. Moi, R. Koch (Paderborn University, Direct Manufacturing Research Center)
earlier_versions: Lindemann, Jahnke, Moi, Koch (2012), 'Analyzing Product Lifecycle Costs for a Better Understanding of Cost Drivers in Additive Manufacturing', SFF Symposium 2012: earlier DMRC cost-driver analysis whose results the 2013 lifecycle-cost paper builds on.
description: Lifecycle cost model following the DIN/IEC 60300-3-3 phases: concept, design and development, production, installation, usage/maintenance, and disposal. Production is costed with time-driven activity-based costing across build-job preparation, build, part and support removal, and post-processing. Build rate, machine cost, material cost and utilization come out as the dominant drivers.
NRE_note: The design and development phase is costed explicitly: component design, QM planning, prototyping and testing, and production planning. Build-job preparation is also costed. The optimized redesign breaks even at about 250-425 pieces (SFF 2013).
Production_note: TD-ABC of machine, material, personnel, energy, consumables and post-processing, with complexity factors per build job (SFF 2013).
QA_Qual_note: QM planning and prototyping/testing appear as design-phase lifecycle costs, but no material/process qualification or certification burden is modelled (SFF 2013).
QA_Insp_note: Quality control is listed among the TD-ABC production cost elements; no NDI/CT or coupon-testing detail seen (SFF 2013).
Storage_note: The usage/maintenance phase includes logistics support with spare-part storage, but the on-demand inventory benefit of AM is not modelled (SFF 2013).
Shared_Capital_note: TD-ABC allocates machine cost by resource time and names utilisation among the most critical cost factors, though utilisation is a single 75% assumption (about 673 parts/yr) that is never varied (SFF 2013).
Shared_Capacity_note: Not addressed.
Speed_note: Lead time is not modelled; aircraft-on-ground cost (about EUR 100,000/day) is discussed only as motivation, and build time appears only as a cost driver (SFF 2013).

name: Atzeni & Salmi DMLS vs. die-casting break-even model
developer: E. Atzeni, A. Salmi (Politecnico di Torino)
description: Builds cost models for DMLS and high-pressure die casting of the same DfAM-redesigned aerospace part to find the volume at which AM becomes competitive. It concludes AM can compete for small-to-medium batches.
NRE_note: The part is redesigned with a DfAM approach (abstract), but the abstract does not show that redesign or engineering cost is included.
Production_note: Per-part cost models for both processes (abstract). Khanna et al. 2024 report machine depreciation was ~90% of the AM part cost.
QA_Qual_note: Only the abstract and a review summary were read; neither mentions qualification or certification of the aeronautical part, so whether it is costed cannot be established.
QA_Insp_note: Only the abstract and a review summary (material, setup, machine, heat-treatment and post-processing labour terms) were read; inspection is not mentioned, but the full model could include it.
Storage_note: The abstract and review describe a per-part production-cost comparison by batch size, and inventory lies outside that documented scope.
Shared_Capital_note: A review reports that machine cost is spread over the parts per build with 5-year straight-line depreciation and is about 90% of AM part cost, but utilisation and nesting choices could not be checked without the full text (Khanna et al. 2024).
Shared_Capacity_note: Not addressed.
Speed_note: Only the abstract and a review summary were read; lead time is not mentioned, but an AM vs. die-casting comparison could plausibly treat tooling lead time.

name: Baumers et al. (2017) total-cost and capacity-utilisation model (IJPR)
developer: M. Baumers, P. Dickens, C. Tuck, R. Hague (University of Nottingham), with L. Beltrametti and A. Gasparre on the 2017 paper
earlier_versions: Baumers, Dickens, Tuck, Hague (2016), Technol. Forecast. Soc. Change 102:193-201: production-cost model for EBM and DMLS (about GBP 2.39 vs. 6.18 per cm3 deposited) showing machine productivity drives cost; the 2017 model adds total cost with build-failure risk, filling build volume with other geometries, and the value of design adaptation.
description: Activity-based production cost models that combine direct costs with time-allocated indirect (machine and overhead) costs, voxel-based build-time estimates, and computational packing of the build volume. The 2017 version adds per-layer build-failure risk and the discounted value of design adaptation. It shows single-geometry builds overstate unit cost by 157% on average compared with full mixed builds.
NRE_note: Design and redesign re-validation costs are explicitly excluded; only per-build machine setup labour (180 min) is included (IJPR 2017 full text).
Production_note: Unit cost = material + energy + time-based indirect cost + setup and post-processing labour; the 17-4PH blower costs ~EUR 56-58/unit in mixed builds (IJPR 2017).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification and re-validation costs are not quantified (IJPR 2017).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection is only lumped into 37 min/part of manual post-processing labour, along with support removal, surface finishing and washing (IJPR 2017).
Storage_note: In-process inventory excluded (IJPR 2017).
Shared_Capital_note: Central contribution: indirect machine cost is allocated by build time and volume share, and filling unused build volume with other geometries ('fungible' capacity) cuts unit cost. Machine productivity is the principal cost driver (TFSC 2016; IJPR 2017).
Shared_Capacity_note: Filling builds with other users' parts is treated only as a cost effect; no lead-time or multi-site capacity analysis.
Speed_note: Lead time explicitly excluded (IJPR 2017).

name: Schröder et al. AM cost-structure / PSS cost-calculation model
developer: M. Schröder, B. Falk, R. Schmitt (RWTH Aachen, WZL)
description: Activity-based model that breaks an AM order into eight main process steps and seven cost categories: design and planning, material, machine setup, manufacturing, post-processing, quality, and administration/sales. Build time is computed from build-envelope and part dimensions using 2D/3D packing.
NRE_note: Design and planning (configuration, slicing, scaling) is a costed category, ~25% (EUR 300 of EUR 1,218) of the example order.
Production_note: Manufacturing, material, setup and post-processing costs are computed per order, with sensitivity analysis on machine cost rate, layer thickness, fill level and post-processing time.
QA_Qual_note: Only the conference slides were read; they cost a 'quality characteristics' category without defining it, so whether qualification or certification is included is not shown.
QA_Insp_note: 'Quality characteristics' is an explicit cost category (~24.5%, EUR 299, in the example order).
Storage_note: The slides give the full seven-category cost breakdown of an AM order (design/planning, material, setup, manufacturing, post-processing, quality, administration/sales), and none covers inventory.
Shared_Capital_note: Machine cost rate depends on investment and workload, and parts per build (2D/3D packing) and fill level are inputs. Economies of scale were found only for small parts.
Shared_Capacity_note: The slides' cost breakdown and packing logic cover one machine's build jobs only; no capacity pooling across sites or users is shown.
Speed_note: The slides' seven cost categories contain no lead-time or delivery-time value; build time is used only to compute cost.

name: Laureijs/Fuchs (CMU) process-based cost model: metal AM vs. forging
developer: R. E. Laureijs, J. Bonnín Roca, S. P. Narra, C. Montgomery, J. L. Beuth, E. R. H. Fuchs (Carnegie Mellon University; E. R. H. Fuchs lab, Engineering & Public Policy)
description: Process-based cost model built on data from 14 anonymous firms (AM producers, powder and equipment suppliers, a university lab) and the Forging Industry Association. The AM route is modelled from the build step through stress relief (DMLS only), wire EDM, HIP, shot peening and destructive testing. At 1,000/yr the AM bracket costs about $3,200 vs. about $400 forged. With a 10-year fuel-saving NPV ($1,300 base, up to $3,000 per bracket), AM is competitive at 2,000-12,000/yr. Powder price and batch size (set by build orientation) are the top sensitivities. Cutting destructive testing from 1 part in 8 to 1 in 100 saves about $150/bracket at 10,000/yr, and about $410 when combined with vertical builds. FAA configuration control is modelled as 'one machine, one part' dedication of the AM machines.
NRE_note: Explicitly excluded. The model assumes the user has already optimised the design and converted it to STL, and it begins at the build step. Redesign enters only as the lighter geometry; its engineering cost is not counted (ASME full text).
Production_note: Per-bracket cost for DMLS, EBM and forging vs. annual volume (1,000-12,000/yr), with process-step inputs, reject rates, and best/base/worst ranges (ASME full text, Figs. 4-7).
QA_Qual_note: FAA production certification and configuration control are not costed in dollars. They are represented as a 'one machine, one part' dedication rule that raises AM machine cost per part below ~2,000/yr. Recertification after process changes is discussed only qualitatively (ASME full text).
QA_Insp_note: Destructive testing is explicitly modelled as a yield loss (base 1 part in 8 destroyed), with a sensitivity sweep (Fig. 8: 1:8 to 1:100 saves ~$150/bracket at 10k/yr). Testing time and equipment are not costed, and NDI/CT is not costed for AM (forging is assumed to use NDT). Borderline Yes for destructive testing only (ASME full text).
Storage_note: Inventory and spares are not analysed. Lead-time reduction appears only in the introduction, plus a footnote on military field repair (ASME full text).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine dedication is an explicit decision rule: AM machines are dedicated to the bracket, while forging equipment is shared with other parts. Batch size per build, which depends on vertical vs. horizontal orientation, is analysed for its cost effect (Fig. 9; ~$260 extra saving). The amortisation period is not stated in the text (ASME full text).
Shared_Capacity_note: Single-site production; no pooling of capacity across sites or users (ASME full text).
Speed_note: Time value is not modelled. The lifecycle benefit is fuel savings from weight reduction, not availability (ASME full text).

name: Bonnín Roca (CMU) process-based cost model + facility-location model for decentralized metal AM
developer: J. Bonnín Roca, P. Vaishnav, R. E. Laureijs, J. Mendonça, E. R. H. Fuchs (Carnegie Mellon University EPP; Universidade de Lisboa / IN+ via CMU Portugal; Bonnín Roca now at TU Eindhoven). M. G. Morgan is not a co-author of this paper; he co-authored the team's regulation papers.
description: A location-dependent process-based cost model (local labour and land costs) feeds an uncapacitated facility-location MILP. The MILP picks the cost-minimising number and location of AM sites, trading production scale economies against transport and inventory costs. The optimal number of sites barely changes across technology-improvement scenarios, and as demand grows the factory moves toward the highest-demand airports. Decentralisation pays only for non-critical parts that can share the same equipment with minimal certification requirements, at combined volumes in the tens of thousands per year. At lower volumes it pays only for parts that need no HIP. Expensive post-processing equipment is what favours centralisation.
NRE_note: Only the abstract, section snippets and news pieces were read; they do not say whether design or build-preparation cost is included, although the predecessor Laureijs model excludes it.
Production_note: Location-dependent PBCM of metal AM production, including post-processing such as HIP (ScienceDirect abstract and snippets; CMU news).
QA_Qual_note: Certification is a scoping and scenario assumption rather than a cost. The model is limited to non-critical parts with 'minimal certification requirements' that can run on shared equipment (the CMU news piece states many part types are assumed to share one machine). This is the reverse of Laureijs 2017's 'one machine, one part' rule. No qualification cost line is visible in the accessed text.
QA_Insp_note: The accessed abstract and snippets do not mention inspection or testing, and whether the Laureijs destructive-testing yield carries over could not be checked.
Storage_note: Inventory cost is an explicit term in the location trade-off, alongside production and transport (abstract). Safety-stock formulation not visible.
Shared_Capital_note: Scale economies per site are the core trade-off. Many part types are assumed to share the same AM equipment (CMU news), and costly post-processing (HIP) equipment favours fewer, shared sites (abstract; CMU news).
Shared_Capacity_note: The MILP chooses the number and location of sites as an uncapacitated facility-location problem. Pooling therefore shows up only through scale economies, transport and inventory cost; there is no capacity constraint and no lead-time or queue effect. Other uncapacitated location models in the survey are rated Partial.
Speed_note: Lead time enters only implicitly, through the transport and inventory costs of distance. There is no dollar value of downtime, readiness or lead time; the introduction cites lead-time reduction only as a motivation (ScienceDirect snippets).

name: Knofius-van der Heijden-Zijm AHP spare-part screening (SINTAS; Fokker, Royal Netherlands forces)
developer: N. Knofius, M. C. van der Heijden, W. H. M. Zijm (University of Twente)
description: Two-level AHP. Company goals (secure supply, reduce downtime, reduce costs) weight part attributes that can be pulled from company databases: safety-stock cost, manufacturing/order cost, demand rate, survival probability, remaining usage period, resupply lead time and airplane type. Go/no-go gates on material and size come first, and the ranking tells the firm which parts to build AM business cases for.
NRE_note: No criterion for 3D data, reverse engineering or redesign effort (thesis Tables 2.1/2.5).
Production_note: Conventional manufacturing/order cost is a scored attribute (17%), used as a proxy for savings potential; no AM cost estimate.
QA_Qual_note: Qualification and certification are not scored; the thesis notes certification cost was high in one case but left it out of the model.
QA_Insp_note: Not addressed.
Storage_note: Safety-stock cost is the highest-weighted attribute (18%) in the screening score. It is a criterion, not an inventory model.
Shared_Capital_note: Not addressed.
Shared_Capacity_note: Not addressed.
Speed_note: Resupply lead time (13%) and a 'reduce downtime' goal are in the AHP hierarchy; downtime is not dollarized.

name: Paderborn DMRC Trade-off Methodology (TOM), 2017 version (Kruse, Reiher & Koch)
developer: C. Lindemann, T. Reiher, U. Jahnke, R. Koch; A. Kruse (Paderborn University, DMRC)
earlier_versions: Lindemann, Jahnke, Reiher & Koch (2014), SFF Symposium paper 'Towards a sustainable and economic selection of part candidates for AM': original workshop-based part-selection matrix with an early cost-estimation module. | Lindemann, Reiher, Jahnke & Koch (2015), Rapid Prototyping Journal 21(2):216-227 (doi:10.1108/RPJ-12-2014-0179): journal version reporting 90% overlap with independent expert selections in an ESA project; the 2017 version adds knock-out gates, four value categories, company and product questionnaires, and an Excel implementation.
description: Three-phase workshop (information, assessment, decision) in which non-experts and AM experts score candidate parts in a trade-off matrix. Criteria cover size limits, part class, assembly suppression, post-processing need, material applicability, design rules, property improvement and processing time, then material change, buy-to-fly, lead time and an AM-vs-milling cost ratio. Redesign and economic evaluation follow, and the 2017 revision adds knock-out gates and four value categories.
NRE_note: Redesign requirement-gathering is part of the method and redesign savings are discussed, but redesign and data-preparation effort are not costed (SFF 2014; RPJ 2015).
Production_note: A relative AM-vs-milling cost ratio and an early cost-estimation module feed the decision phase; a full cost comparison is only planned in the 2017 version (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).
QA_Qual_note: Material applicability (industry use, public data) and space-specific requirements are scored; no formal certification step (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).
QA_Insp_note: Not a criterion.
Storage_note: Savings on tooling and tool warehousing are mentioned, and the 2017 questionnaire asks about spare-part management strategy; no spares-inventory criterion.
Shared_Capital_note: Machine availability (in-house or provider) is only a size-feasibility check.
Shared_Capacity_note: Not addressed.
Speed_note: Lead, process and post-processing time, and time-criticality, are scored criteria (SFF 2014).

name: VTT/Aalto digital spare parts program (DIVA / DIVALIITO): screening, metal PBF cost tool, qualification workflow
developer: M. Salmi, J. Partanen, J. Tuomi, S. Chekurov, N. Kretzschmar et al. (Aalto University); S. Metsä-Kortelainen, A. Jussila et al. (VTT)
description: Four-phase spare-part classification adapted from Knofius et al.: technical (material, size), photo-based geometry review, ranking, then economic (price, resupply lead time, annual consumption, MOQ). Only ~2% of one firm's items were feasible. It adds an STL-based metal PBF cost tool and illustrative AM vs. conventional business cases that include downtime. Its cost tool was later released as AMDSP 2.0, which is listed separately.
NRE_note: 3D-model availability is listed as a technical criterion; digitisation and redesign are not costed.
Production_note: MATLAB STL-based metal PBF cost tool: machine amortisation (8 yr), labour, material, packing ratio, powder recycling, follow-up time. Case costs include an Inconel 718 pin at ~EUR 55 vs. EUR 90.
QA_Qual_note: Certified printers and processes, approvals, and liability for safety-critical parts are discussed as barriers; not costed.
QA_Insp_note: The DIVA report lists hardness, porosity, Charpy, tensile, chemistry and functional tests on printed parts, but does not cost them.
Storage_note: The enclosure business case quantifies inventory reduction from printing on demand: average stock 10 vs 1 pcs, storage cost EUR 100 vs EUR 1, plus replenishment batch and logistics-to-stock costs (DIVA report Table 4). This is the same case that supports the Speed rating.
Shared_Capital_note: The PBF cost tool depreciates the printer over 8 years, but the 74% figure is the powder packing ratio, not part nesting. No utilisation, operating-hours or parts-per-build input is described. Spreading capital through service providers' 'wider customer base' is mentioned only qualitatively (DIVA report).
Shared_Capacity_note: The companion survey (Kretzschmar et al. 2018) sketches centralized and distributed digital spare-part network scenarios qualitatively.
Speed_note: The enclosure business case quantifies downtime (EUR 1,000/h) and a 20-day delivery time to show AM can be cheaper overall; re-supply lead time is a screening criterion.

name: Chaudhuri et al. design-science spare-part selection (TOPSIS + clustering + AHP)
developer: A. Chaudhuri, H. A. Gerlich, J. Jayaram, A. Ghadge, J. Shack, B. H. Brix, L. H. Hoffbeck, N. Ulriksen
description: Database filters (size, time to stock-out, overhead cost, obsolescence, unit cost), then two-step cluster analysis and AHP ranking of clusters with weights from a management workshop (service 72%, cost 22%, other 6%). Parts are ranked with TOPSIS within clusters and finally reviewed against technical drawings.
NRE_note: Availability of technical drawings acted as a de facto gate (only 54 of 100 sampled parts had them); digitisation effort not costed.
Production_note: Unit (standard) cost is a filter and an AHP sub-weight; no AM cost model.
QA_Qual_note: Certification is not a criterion.
QA_Insp_note: Not addressed.
Storage_note: Overhead cost (inventory + transport), inventory-cost and obsolescence weights, and a time-to-stock-out filter are used for ranking and screening.
Shared_Capital_note: Not addressed.
Shared_Capacity_note: Not addressed.
Speed_note: Lead time is a ranking criterion and availability is weighted 51% within service.

name: McGill automated AM part-candidate decision support (Yang, Page, Zhang & Zhao 2020)
developer: T. D. Page, S. Yang, Y. Zhang, Y. F. Zhao (McGill University)
earlier_versions: Page, Yang & Zhao, 'Automated Candidate Detection for Additive Manufacturing: A Framework Proposal', ICED 2019 (doi:10.1017/dsi.2019.72): framework proposal comparing six classifiers on ~120 expert-labelled parts; all ratings in this entry rest on this paper's full text, as the 2020 JIM article (which extends it toward a decision-support system) was not readable.
description: Machine-learning decision model (a decision tree, best of six sklearn classifiers). It combines ERP economic data (production cost, batch size, inventory cost, import/export, sole-sourcing), CAD complexity ratios and user-answered AM-potential questions to flag economic feasibility and six AM potentials for expert review.
NRE_note: Not addressed.
Production_note: Production cost ($/part) is a criterion; the case study used SolidWorks Costing estimates for AM vs. machining (ICED 2019).
QA_Qual_note: Not addressed (ICED 2019).
QA_Insp_note: Not addressed.
Storage_note: Inventory cost is an economic input criterion.
Shared_Capital_note: Not addressed.
Shared_Capacity_note: Not addressed.
Speed_note: Lead time is used as an economic criterion in the case study (it is not in Table 2).

name: Yang & Zhao lifecycle part-count-reduction (consolidation) method
developer: S. Yang, Y. F. Zhao (McGill University)
description: Treats part consolidation as a combinatorial optimization that minimizes the lifecycle cost/performance ratio under manufacturing, maintenance and recycling constraints. It is solved with a two-level grouping-and-refinement framework plus part-count-reduction design rules.
NRE_note: Redesign rules are central, but design effort is not costed.
Production_note: Manufacturing difficulty is a constraint and assembly cost reduction is in the lifecycle objective; no machine- or material-level cost model seen.
QA_Qual_note: Only the JMD featured-article abstract was read; it does not say whether qualification enters the lifecycle cost/performance objective.
QA_Insp_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not say whether inspection is part of the lifecycle cost.
Storage_note: Only the abstract was read; inventory is not mentioned, but a lifecycle objective for reducing part count could plausibly include it.
Shared_Capital_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not say whether machine cost or build packing enters the manufacturing term.
Shared_Capacity_note: Not addressed.
Speed_note: Only the abstract was read; maintenance is a constraint, but it does not say whether downtime or lead time is valued.

name: Ghiasian et al. (2020) preference-based AM design-readiness assessment
developer: S. E. Ghiasian, P. Jaiswal, R. Rai, K. Lewis (University at Buffalo)
earlier_versions: Ghiasian, Jaiswal, Rai, Lewis (2018), ASME IDETC DETC2018-86238 (doi:10.1115/DETC2018-86238): voxel-based fabrication-feasibility framework (geometry, build orientation and supports, resource cost and time) tested on 34 parts; the 2020 version adds multi-criteria readiness scoring with physical-programming preference functions.
description: Voxel-based framework that judges AM feasibility on geometry, build orientation and support generation, and resource needs (cost and time). The 2020 version scores multi-criteria AM readiness with physical-programming preference functions.
NRE_note: Build orientation and support generation (build preparation) are evaluated and design modification is considered; no one-time engineering cost.
Production_note: Resource requirements (cost and time) are one feasibility perspective; the level of cost detail is not visible in the abstracts.
QA_Qual_note: Only the abstracts were read and the 2020 multi-criteria readiness criteria are not listed, so whether certification is a criterion cannot be established.
QA_Insp_note: Only the abstracts were read and the readiness criteria are not listed, so whether inspection or post-processing is assessed cannot be established.
Storage_note: Not addressed.
Shared_Capital_note: The abstracts name resource cost as a feasibility perspective but do not show whether machine cost or build sharing enters it.
Shared_Capacity_note: Not addressed.
Speed_note: Time is a resource requirement in the 2018 framework, but the abstracts do not show whether lead time is compared or valued.

name: Purdue Design for AM (DfAM) Worksheet
developer: J. W. Booth, J. Alperovich, P. Chawla, J. Ma, T. N. Reid, K. Ramani (Purdue University)
description: One-page visual worksheet, built from common mistakes identified by expert machinists and AM facilities, that rates a part's likely print quality and suggests redesign. Used as a go/no-go filter, it cut poorly designed submissions by 81%.
NRE_note: Prompts redesign before printing, which avoids wasted builds; design effort is not quantified.
Production_note: No cost estimate; cost appears only in the classroom-study discussion.
QA_Qual_note: Not addressed.
QA_Insp_note: Rates a design's 'potential quality', not inspection.
Storage_note: Not addressed.
Shared_Capital_note: Not addressed.
Shared_Capacity_note: Not addressed.
Speed_note: Not addressed.

name: Klahn-Leutenecker-Meboldt (ETH Zurich) design-strategy and indicator method
developer: C. Klahn, B. Leutenecker, M. Meboldt (ETH Zurich; inspire AG)
description: Separates a manufacturing-driven strategy (substituting AM for an existing process, possibly later in the lifecycle) from a function-driven strategy (redesign for performance). It proposes indicators for parts that gain most from AM through process advantages vs. design advantages.
NRE_note: The strategy choice sets how much redesign is warranted, and function-driven redesign is described as a major effort, but it is not quantified (Procedia CIRP full text).
Production_note: Upgraded after reading the Procedia CIRP full text: cost is a screening outcome and a reason for the manufacturing-driven strategy, and a polymer case compares quoted unit cost by lot size (Fig. 4), but there is no cost model.
QA_Qual_note: Not addressed.
QA_Insp_note: Not addressed.
Storage_note: The Procedia CIRP paper does not discuss inventory, but the companion ICED 2015 indicators paper was read only as an abstract, so an inventory or spare-parts indicator cannot be ruled out.
Shared_Capital_note: Not addressed.
Shared_Capacity_note: Not addressed.
Speed_note: Upgraded after reading the Procedia CIRP full text: the manufacturing-driven strategy uses AM for time reasons (about 3 weeks vs. 3 months for an injection-mould tool in the case), but time is not valued.

name: Purdue/Virginia Tech Decision Engine for AM in defense acquisition
developer: W. Tsutsui, Q. Shi, I. Walter, A. Wei, C. Williams, D. DeLaurentis, J. Panchal (Purdue University; Virginia Tech)
description: Expected-utility engine that ranks AM and conventional routes on total cost, total time and part mass, with a bounding-box go/no-go check. Cost comes from a Gibson et al.-style model (prorated machine purchase, operation, material, labour). Hybrid WAAM ranked highest in both scenarios.
NRE_note: The topology-optimized redesign scenario changes mass and cost, but redesign effort is not costed.
