name: DoDI 5000.93 Use of Additive Manufacturing in the DoD (Change 1, July 6, 2021)
developer: OUSD(R&E) (approved by Barbara McQuiston); incorporates and cancels DTM-19-006
earlier_versions: DTM-19-006 'Interim Policy and Guidance for the Use of Additive Manufacturing (AM) in Support of Materiel Sustainment' (March 21, 2019): interim directive-type memorandum, incorporated and cancelled by DoDI 5000.93. | DoDI 5000.93 original issuance (June 10, 2021): Change 1 (July 6, 2021) only removed a duplicate responsibility entry in paragraph 2.3.
description: The instruction requires a 'risk-informed approach' but prescribes no decision method, scoring model or cost-benefit tool. Maintenance activities must 'consider and evaluate AM's technical and economic practicality.' Contracts should identify parts that 'are, or could be, produced using AM.' Organizations that share approved AM data across organizations must adopt JAMMEX.
NRE_note: Directs buying only the AM data and license rights needed (§3.1.c) and flagging AM-capable parts in the bill of materials (§3.1.d). TDP creation and reverse engineering are not costed.
Production_note: Requires evaluating 'technical and economic practicality' (§3.3.c) but gives no cost method.
QA_Qual_note: Policies must define 'the level of qualification, certification, risk evaluation, and approval authority' for AM parts (§3.2.a). Not costed.
QA_Insp_note: Parts must 'comply with established quality control criteria' (§3.2.d), and AM data must include 'testing requirements and acceptance or rejection criteria' (§3.1.b(2)). Not costed.
Storage_note: Inventory or stock reduction is not addressed. JAMMEX is framed only as a data-sharing portal.
Shared_Capital_note: Not addressed.
Shared_Capacity_note: USD(A&S) must ensure 'adequate and uninterrupted AM capacity' in the domestic base (§2.3.e). Pooling across sites or units is not addressed.
Speed_note: Calls for making parts 'consistent with demand urgency' (§3.3.b) and in contingency or combat environments to improve readiness. Not quantified.

name: RAND 3D printing supply-chain impact matrix and fab-lab concept (PE-229)
developer: RAND Corporation (Simon Véronneau, Geoffrey Torrington, Jakub P. Hlavka)
description: A two-by-two matrix in which the impact of 3D printing grows with site isolation and with ad hoc (unpredictable) demand. The paper proposes a four-machine fab-lab and a process flow: incoming inspection, CT, 3D rendering, AM or CNC, post-production, outgoing inspection, tracking and serialization, then return to service. It calls for a total supply-chain cost comparison but gives no cost model and does not rank parts.
NRE_note: CT metrology can 'generate a 3D printable design' from existing parts. Characterizing a part without a 3D diagram 'would take about one hour.' Not costed.
Production_note: Says a fab-lab vs centralized comparison 'must involve a total supply chain cost approach' and calls for a 'comprehensive cost-effectiveness evaluation'. No per-part cost.
QA_Qual_note: Recommends 'rationalizing the certification and testing approach' for AM components. Qualitative.
QA_Insp_note: Incoming and outgoing inspection and CT scanning are steps in the process flow, and CT is called 'relatively underappreciated'. Not costed.
Storage_note: The full text does not discuss inventory, stock or holding cost; it mentions only secure storage of part design files.
Shared_Capital_note: The full text mentions civilian fab-labs used 'on a pay-per-use basis' but does not cost the proposed fab-lab or discuss sharing its equipment.
Shared_Capacity_note: The matrix argues for forward fab-labs at isolated sites with ad hoc demand rather than central production. Qualitative.
Speed_note: Times only: a noncritical part 'in as little as 45 minutes', and readiness gains where items 'cannot otherwise be procured'. Not valued.

name: RAND Europe AM and obsolescence management in defence (PE-171), with Cranfield obsolescence-resolution cost metrics
developer: RAND Europe (eds. Jon Freeman, Giacomo Persi Paoli). Contributors from armasuisse S+T, US Army ARDEC (G. Di Benedetto) and Cranfield University (J. Erkoyuncu, R. Roy, S. Williams, P. Colegrove, F. Martina, A. Busachi). Funded by armasuisse S+T.
description: A collection of expert perspectives, not a model. The nearest decision elements are a 'window of opportunity' test for obsolescence, a list of resolution options (same component, form-fit-function replacement, emulation, redesign), and Cranfield cost metrics (Table 2) for choosing 'the most cost effective solution'. The cost metrics are not AM-specific.
NRE_note: Cranfield Table 2 quantifies non-recurring obsolescence-resolution costs by integration level, for example emulation from £52,100 (small) to £2.69m (very large). These are not AM-specific. The US Navy RESTORE 'SCAN to CAD to FAB' workflow is described without costs.
Production_note: Says small batches can be made 'on-demand at a constant cost' and that costs are 'largely predictable'. No unit figures.
QA_Qual_note: Requalification costs appear in the generic resolution-cost table. DMLS 4340 tensile data approach wrought properties. No AM qualification costing.
QA_Insp_note: Not addressed.
Storage_note: Proposes digital storage of designs instead of physical stock. The cost table includes existing stock (£300 per case). This is not an AM inventory model.
Shared_Capital_note: Not addressed.
Shared_Capacity_note: Mobile AM facilities are suggested for sustainment contracts. No pooling.
Speed_note: Anecdote: some FRCE repairs were made with AM 'over a few days' instead of three or more weeks. The window-of-opportunity concept is not valued.

name: NASA In-Space Manufacturing spares-logistics case (MSFC briefings citing Owens & de Weck 2016 and Cirillo et al. 2011)
developer: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center In-Space Manufacturing (ISM) project (R. G. Clinton Jr.; T. Prater, N. Werkheiser, F. Ledbetter), citing analyses by Owens & de Weck (2016) and Cirillo et al. (2011)
description: NASA's case for ISM rests on spares logistics. About 95% of corrective spares will never be used, and about 3,000 kg/yr of upmass compares with about 18,000 kg of ground spares ready to fly. Cited analyses report spares-mass cuts of 78.3% (ISM plus recycling) and 97.7% (the Owens & de Weck case). For a fluid-flow parts case, about one-third of components were assumed printable in space. No other NASA cost or part-selection tool was found besides NASA-STD-6030, which is scored elsewhere.
NRE_note: Only MSFC briefings were read and the underlying Owens & de Weck and Cirillo analyses were not opened; the briefings do not mention design or engineering effort.
Production_note: The briefings give no per-part cost for in-space manufacturing, and the underlying analyses, which were not opened, may or may not include cost.
QA_Qual_note: Briefings describe qualifying the metallurgical process on each AM machine, and list 'Verification & Certification Processes' as still under development. Not costed (NASA-STD-6030 is scored elsewhere).
QA_Insp_note: In-space NDE is listed as a gap. ISM specimens are inspected by structured-light scanning (±12.7 µm), CT, microscopy and mechanical tests. Not costed.
Storage_note: Cited analyses quantify spares-mass reduction (78.3%; 97.7%), motivated by ~95% of corrective spares never being used. Reported secondhand in NASA briefings.
Shared_Capital_note: The briefings do not address printer cost or sharing, and the underlying analyses were not opened.
Shared_Capacity_note: The briefings call the ISS Additive Manufacturing Facility a 'multi-user facility' but do not model capacity, and the underlying analyses were not opened.
Speed_note: The briefings report spares mass rather than time to part or availability, and the underlying analyses, which were not opened, may model availability.

name: Meisel et al. decision support for AM deployment in remote or austere environments (tiered-funnel machine/material selector)
developer: Nicholas A. Meisel, Christopher B. Williams, Kimberly P. Ellis, Don Taylor. Affiliations are not shown in the record opened; C. B. Williams is Virginia Tech per the LMI/DLA entry.
description: An interview-derived framework for deployable AM. User constraints fall into process, machine, part, material, environmental and logistical categories, and these feed a 'tiered funnel' tool that narrows a database of candidate machines and materials. The paper calls itself a 'user-driven tool for selecting a process and material'. Scores are from the abstract only.
NRE_note: Only the abstract was read (the Emerald full text is behind a bot check); it does not say whether design or engineering effort is a funnel criterion.
Production_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not say whether machine or material cost is a funnel attribute.
QA_Qual_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not say whether qualification or part-quality requirements are funnel criteria.
QA_Insp_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not mention inspection.
Storage_note: Motivation only: AM 'can reduce the process supply chain' by making spare parts from one raw-material source. Not quantified.
Shared_Capital_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not mention equipment cost or sharing.
Shared_Capacity_note: Only the abstract was read; it selects equipment for a deployment and does not say whether capacity across sites is considered.
Speed_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not say whether build time or time to part is a criterion.

name: Braunberger AFIT MODA and metal L-PBF cost model for AM vs DLA procurement (C-130 parts)
developer: 1st Lt Trever J. Braunberger, USAF, Air Force Institute of Technology (committee: Maj John Situ, Maj Ryan Kemnitz, Alfred E. Thal Jr.)
description: A nine-criterion multi-objective decision analysis. Weights: quality 21.0%, lead time 20.1%, readiness 18.3%, price 14.6%, airworthiness 7.3%, expected life 6.3%, strength 6.2%, weight 4.8%, quantity 1.5%. Score bands: 86–100% is an 'extremely good candidate'; below 60%, use traditional methods. It is paired with an Atzeni & Salmi-based cost model and a guide to AM lab set-up costs ($1.94M for one metal lab). Single-part AM builds averaged $3,174.96 against $2,486.83 DLA prices, 27.6% more. Table 4.3 shows two of six parts cheaper with AM, while the text says three. AM lead times were 9–16 days against 71 to 120+ days.
NRE_note: Pre-processing cost CPRE = (ET x EC) + (TS x CO) includes an engineering-time term, and the thesis says NRE ('reengineering required to print a part, including creating digital 3D data, and programming') was included. Per-part pre-processing costs ($69-150, Table 4.3) exceed the $43.80 setup term, so engineering time is costed, although ET/EC values are not stated. Reverse engineering (150+ h) and parameter development (6+ months, $150k+) are listed but not allocated.
Production_note: Per-part material, pre-processing, processing (build-time formula, depreciation, energy, maintenance) and post-processing (labor $21.9/h, heat treatment $85/part). Results for six parts and for batch builds.
QA_Qual_note: Airworthiness is a MODA criterion (7.3% weight) and parameter-development testing costs are noted. Airworthiness approval is not costed and is called 'challenging and difficult'.
QA_Insp_note: Tensile test per build, with test-sample volume in material cost and $1,061 grips. Volumetric and NDI inspection are not included.
Storage_note: Notes that 'space does cost money', but storage and transport savings are called 'difficult to quantify' and are not modeled.
Shared_Capital_note: Depreciation of the ~$1.105M machine is charged per build hour (CDEP/MH, 8-year life). Multi-part builds are costed explicitly, cutting per-part cost by 33% (2 parachute racks) and 35% (3 bracket mounts) (Table 4.4). Sharing across sites or users is not modeled.
Shared_Capacity_note: Qualitative only: SME interviews call for a printer network and note distributed production 'may be cost effective' with more automation; no capacity pooling is modeled.
Speed_note: Lead time is compared per part (AM 9–16 days vs DLA 71 to 120+ days) and scored in the MODA alongside a separate readiness criterion. Time is quantified, not dollarized.

name: Crean AFIT metal AM per-part cost model and AM capability fielding costs
developer: Capt Ryan C. Crean, USAF, Air Force Institute of Technology (advisor Alan W. Johnson)
description: An Atzeni & Salmi-based cost model (material, pre-processing, processing, post-processing) with a layer-based build-time formula. It matched UDRI builds within 0–5.3%. Single builds averaged $3,144.74 per part and maximum batches $2,615.95. Before NRE, only 1 of 7 parts was cheaper with AM in single builds, and 3 with batching. Fielding one metal capability costs about $1.52–1.66M per alloy family.
NRE_note: Excluded from per-part cost, though the author says it 'will drive up the overall cost significantly'. Cites an AFLCMC estimate of '$1,000,000 to complete the NRE'. Build prep is $90 per build.
Production_note: Per part: material, depreciation (~$1.1M machine), maintenance ($18k/yr), energy, labor ($45/h) and heat treatment ($100). Cost shares are reported (machine 35%, post-processing 36%).
QA_Qual_note: Notes that AM process specifications do not yet exist, a barrier. Not costed.
QA_Insp_note: An ASTM E8 tensile coupon per build is costed at $300. Volumetric inspection is excluded. A CMM (~$100k) is listed.
Storage_note: Holding and transport savings are said to vary by part and location; not modeled.
Shared_Capital_note: Machine depreciation spread over machine-hours, batches of up to 16 parts per build, one machine per alloy family. No portfolio or user sharing.
Shared_Capacity_note: Pooling across sites is not modeled. A networked parts library is discussed qualitatively.
Speed_note: Current PLT+ALT is reported for each part (324–611 days), but AM lead time and readiness are not in the model.

name: Draudt AFIT Advanced Intermediate Manufacturing (AIM) facility supply-chain simulation
developer: Eric S. Draudt, Air Force Institute of Technology (advisor Frank W. Ciarallo)
description: An anyLogistix simulation comparing the current supply chain with single, dual and quadruple AIM facilities and with high, medium and low utilization. A single facility cuts lead time from over 800 days to about 104 days. The thesis recommends starting with one facility to keep investment costs under control.
NRE_note: Only the abstract could be read (the full PDF fails to load); it does not mention engineering or reverse-engineering effort.
Production_note: Only the abstract could be read; it mentions investment costs but not production cost.
QA_Qual_note: Only the abstract could be read; it does not mention qualification.
QA_Insp_note: Only the abstract could be read; it does not mention inspection.
Storage_note: Only the abstract could be read; it does not say whether inventory is modeled in the anyLogistix simulation.
Shared_Capital_note: Investment cost is the stated reason to start with one facility. Not quantified in the abstract.
Shared_Capacity_note: Simulates the number of facilities (1, 2 or 4) and utilization levels against lead time.
Speed_note: Lead time quantified (over 800 to about 104 days). Time, not dollarized readiness.

name: Daugherty & Heiple NPS USMC AM cost-benefit analysis (extrusion vs CLIP vs OEM supply)
developer: Capt Zachary E. Daugherty and Capt Andrew J. Heiple, USMC (Naval Postgraduate School Acquisition Research Program, NPS-LM-18-018)
description: A cost-benefit analysis comparing OEM parts from the supply system with two AM options. It monetizes costs and the value of time (four valuation methods; Valuation 3 preferred) and compares NPVs in 2017 dollars. Sensitivity cases: baseline, time valuation, reduced days deadlined and equalized initial investment. AM has a production-level cost advantage, with CLIP ahead in 3 of 4 scenarios. Recommends a repository of printable files and continued Fortus use. The NPV tables were not in the text read.
NRE_note: Design and scanning examples are reported (4 h to design an NVG mount; a $25k scanner). Whether they enter the CBA was not verified.
Production_note: Production-level AM and OEM costs are monetized (material, initial investment), showing an AM cost advantage.
QA_Qual_note: Upgraded: the report discusses the parts approval process (slow organizational-level approval; MCSC and I&L vetting of fit, form and function) qualitatively; whether approval costs enter the CBA is not shown in the text read.
QA_Insp_note: Upgraded: the report describes testing printed parts for quality assurance (fit, form and function checks; a fan tested to standard) qualitatively; no inspection cost appears in the text read.
Storage_note: Stocking, transport and retrograde costs are discussed qualitatively, citing the Appleton report.
Shared_Capital_note: Initial investment is in the NPV, with an equalized-investment sensitivity case. No sharing across units.
Shared_Capacity_note: Recommends echeloning printers by maintenance level. Not modeled.
Speed_note: Days deadlined are valued in dollars (four valuation methods), included in NPV and tested in sensitivity cases.

name: AMPAT (Additive Manufacturing Process and Analysis Tool), NPS Navy Expeditionary AM capstone
developer: Leslie J. Amodeo, Brian B. Dick, Charles P. Flynn, Rebecca A. Nagurney and Meagan B. Parker (NPS Systems Engineering capstone). Sponsor: Navy Expeditionary Combat Command (NECC).
description: The user filters a database of AM systems on attributes such as build size, material, process, footprint, print speed, cooling, print quality, post-processing, failure rate, operational availability and environment, then assigns weights. The tool outputs a normalized weighted ranking and plots, for example overall score against initial cost. It covers equipment only, not part selection.
NRE_note: Not addressed. A 3D scanner in the X-FAB is mentioned.
Production_note: Per-part cost is not modeled.
QA_Qual_note: The report recommends a strategy document for approving AM systems for DoD use. The tool has no qualification attribute.
QA_Insp_note: Part validation is discussed qualitatively in the report. Not in the tool.
Storage_note: Fewer spare components are cited as a benefit. Not quantified.
Shared_Capital_note: Machine initial cost appears only as a plotted attribute. No amortization.
Shared_Capacity_note: Meant to inform dispersion and prepositioning of AM assets, which is recommended for future analysis. Not modeled.
Speed_note: Print speed and system operational availability are user-weighted attributes. Part-level readiness appears only as an anecdote (Steel Knight 2016).

name: Holmström et al. rapid-manufacturing capacity-deployment alternatives for spare parts
developer: Jan Holmström, Jouni Partanen, Jukka Tuomi, Manfred Walter
description: A conceptual comparison of centralized rapid-manufacturing (RM) deployment by OEMs with distributed deployment near the point of use by generalist service providers. One variant replaces regional distribution-center inventory with AM capacity. Distributed RM could improve service and cut inventory at the same time, but centralized OEM deployment is judged most feasible. RM spares supply is feasible only in particular situations because few parts can be made. Khajavi et al. (2018) note the authors did not use a case study to show which alternatives are feasible.
NRE_note: Only the abstract and secondary descriptions were read (full text paywalled); none mention design or engineering effort.
Production_note: Production cost is listed as a qualitative consideration (Abidar & Chaabane review table).
QA_Qual_note: Only the abstract and secondary descriptions were read; they do not mention qualification.
QA_Insp_note: Only the abstract and secondary descriptions were read; they do not mention inspection.
Storage_note: Inventory reduction and obsolescence are discussed qualitatively. Not quantified.
Shared_Capital_note: Khajavi et al. (2018) report that the authors judged decentralized deployment possible when AM machine utilization is high; qualitative.
Shared_Capacity_note: The core contribution is the alternative capacity-deployment configurations (central vs point of use). No model.
Speed_note: Better service from point-of-use deployment. Qualitative.

name: Sirichakwal & Conner AM spare-parts inventory model
developer: I. Sirichakwal, B. Conner (affiliations not verified)
description: According to Knofius et al. (2021), the model assumes AM reduces holding costs and lead times and evaluates the effect on stock-out probability. It finds that 'holding cost reductions typically reduce the stock-out probability'. It does not consider cost, so the monetary effect is unclear.
NRE_note: The paper was not opened, and Knofius et al. (2021) do not say whether design or engineering effort is modeled.
Production_note: Knofius et al. (2021) state the model does not consider cost, so production cost is outside its documented scope.
QA_Qual_note: The paper was not opened, and Knofius et al. (2021) do not say whether qualification is addressed.
QA_Insp_note: The paper was not opened, and Knofius et al. (2021) do not say whether inspection is addressed.
Storage_note: Lower holding cost and lead time are assumed inputs. Inventory effects are not monetized.
Shared_Capital_note: The paper was not opened, and Knofius et al. (2021) do not say whether equipment investment is addressed.
Shared_Capacity_note: The paper was not opened, and Knofius et al. (2021) do not say whether AM capacity is modeled.
Speed_note: Stock-out probability is the evaluated output (secondhand description).

name: Kunovjanek & Reiner AM diffusion and raw-material inventory model
developer: Maximilian Kunovjanek, Gerald Reiner
description: A dynamic evaluation model that uses the Bass diffusion model to estimate how AM adoption changes raw-material inventories. AM can cut raw-material inventory by about 4%, and the speed of diffusion depends on the technology's utility. It is not a spare-parts model. The user may instead mean Kunovjanek et al. (2020), 'Additive manufacturing and supply chains – a systematic review', which Abidar & Chaabane cite.
NRE_note: Only the abstract was read (the paper is paywalled); it does not say whether design or engineering effort is part of the model.
Production_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not describe the model's cost components.
QA_Qual_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not mention qualification.
QA_Insp_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not mention inspection.
Storage_note: Quantifies a ~4% raw-material inventory cut, but the mechanism is lower material use, not printing spares on demand.
Shared_Capital_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not say whether equipment investment or its sharing is modeled.
Shared_Capacity_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not mention capacity or pooling.
Speed_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not say whether lead time or availability is modeled.

name: Chekurov et al. perceived value of AM digital spare parts (focus groups and a conceptual distribution network)
developer: Sergei Chekurov, Sini Metsä-Kortelainen, Mika Salmi, Irene Roda, Ari Jussila. Related to the VTT/Aalto DIVA project scored elsewhere; individual affiliations not verified.
description: Checks the literature's claimed benefits of digital spare parts against industry experience. It surfaces post-processing needs, supplier quality parity, and ICT and file-format gaps, and builds a conceptual distribution network for digital spare parts. OEMs estimated that 2–75% of their spare-parts libraries could be printed, with most estimates at 5–10%. The paper concludes that long-tail parts are deployable now.
NRE_note: Missing 3D models, extra modelling work, scanning imprecision and file version management are raised as obstacles. Not costed.
Production_note: AM unit cost is an obstacle that warehousing and transport savings may offset for long-tail parts. Qualitative.
QA_Qual_note: Supplier quality parity is raised as a limitation. Qualification appears only as a literature-based obstacle.
QA_Insp_note: Upgraded: the paper states that for the strictest applications each manufactured material batch requires quality verification, and participants raised varying part quality as an obstacle; inspection is not costed.
Storage_note: Lower inventory and holding cost is confirmed as a perceived benefit. Not quantified.
Shared_Capital_note: Upgraded: participants proposed a jointly owned, centralized machine pool and selling machine time to smaller companies; qualitative only.
Shared_Capacity_note: A conceptual distribution network built from participant input. No capacity model.
Speed_note: Shorter delivery and repair times are confirmed as perceived benefits. Not quantified.

name: Sasson & Johnson 3D printing supercenters concept
developer: Amir Sasson, John Chandler Johnson (BI Norwegian Business School)
description: An invited conceptual paper. Firms use direct digital manufacturing (DDM) to separate out low-volume, disruptive parts even at a higher unit cost, then grow into regional multi-product 'supercenters'. These move spares inventory from finished goods at company plants to raw material at shared DDM facilities. There is no quantitative model; the authors call for cost comparisons and simulation studies.
NRE_note: Not addressed.
Production_note: Accepts higher unit cost for low-volume parts. Qualitative.
QA_Qual_note: Not addressed.
QA_Insp_note: Not addressed.
Storage_note: Finished-goods spares are replaced by raw-material stock at shared facilities. Qualitative.
Shared_Capital_note: Supercenters can 'increase capacity utilization through on-demand printing to other firms', with economies of scope. Qualitative.
Shared_Capacity_note: When one printing center is full, orders are 'redirected to center B'. Qualitative pooling.
Speed_note: Expedite orders for sporadic-demand parts go to 3D printing, and local printing shortens delivery. Qualitative.

name: Strong et al. hybrid-AM hub facility-location model (uncapacitated and p-median, 2018)
developer: Danielle Strong, Michael Kay, Brett Conner, Thomas Wakefield, Guha Manogharan (Penn State)
description: An uncapacitated facility-location model places hubs by geography, demand and hybrid-AM processing cost. Hubs land at demand centroids, and location depends only on AM utilization rate. A constrained p-median model grows from 22 to 44 hubs as demand rises. Outputs are candidate US counties, fixed, operating and transport costs, and hub utilization. Transport cost was not a significant factor.
NRE_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not mention design or engineering effort.
Production_note: Hybrid-AM processing and operating cost at the hub level, not per part.
QA_Qual_note: Only the abstract was read; it mentions meeting GD&T and property requirements but not qualification.
QA_Insp_note: Only the abstract was read; it names post-processing steps but not inspection.
Storage_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not mention inventory.
Shared_Capital_note: Fixed hub cost is traded against the number of hubs, and the spare capacity of traditional shops is pooled into hubs.
Shared_Capacity_note: Hub capacity utilization is an output. The effect on lead time is not modeled.
Speed_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not mention lead time or delivery time.

name: Durão et al. distributed AM spare-parts production use cases (Germany–Brazil network)
developer: Luiz Fernando C. S. Durão, Alexander Christ, Eduardo Zancul, Reiner Anderl, Klaus Schützer
description: A use-case study of how centralization and independence change between a central factory and a distributed AM site. Connected technologies created a flexible, focused factory near the client, with specialization kept at the central factory. Work organization, network performance and IP protection are also evaluated.
NRE_note: Product models come from the central design center, and information exchange between sites is the main challenge. Not costed.
Production_note: Only the abstract was read (full text paywalled); it does not say whether production cost is analyzed.
QA_Qual_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not mention qualification.
QA_Insp_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not mention inspection or quality control.
Storage_note: Only the abstract was read; it cites lower logistics cost but does not mention inventory.
Shared_Capital_note: Only the abstract was read; it does not say whether machine investment at the distributed site is discussed.

name: Muir & Haddud AM impact on spare-parts inventory performance (mechanical engineering and medical industries)
developer: M. Muir, A. Haddud (affiliations not verified)
description: Investigates 'the possible impact of AM adoption on inventory performance and customer satisfaction in a spare parts supply chain' and concludes that 'AM has the potential to improve a firm's inventory performance' (Abidar & Chaabane). It is cited for lead-time and inventory-cost reduction as AM objectives (Durham review). The research method was not verified.

name: Zanoni et al. supply chain implications of AM: case-study synthesis
developer: Simone Zanoni, Milad Ashourpour, Andrea Bacchetti, Massimo Zanardini, Marco Perona (University of Brescia)
description: Synthesizes qualitative and quantitative cases to argue that AM must be assessed across every supply chain stage and lifecycle phase (design, preparation, production, use). It finds that AM vs conventional comparisons are 'exhaustive only when all features of productions and logistics networks are evaluated simultaneously'.

name: Ashour Pour et al. (2019) JELS model of AM in a two-level supply chain
developer: Milad Ashour Pour, Simone Zanoni, Andrea Bacchetti, Massimo Zanardini, Marco Perona (University of Brescia)
earlier_versions: 'Additive Manufacturing Supply Chain: Modeling and Performance Evaluation' (2016), Nineteenth International Working Seminar on Production Economics, vol. 3, pp. 25-36: conference version of the same JELS model, adding discussion of centralized vs decentralized manufacturing; the journal article was first published online in 2017.
description: A JELS analytic model that compares traditional and AM supply chains using the same parameters, from inventory and logistics standpoints. The 2016 proceedings version also gives insights on centralized vs decentralized manufacturing. A review table classifies 'Ashour Pour et al. description: Builds a simple per-specimen CT cost estimate. In-house 220 kV CT: $600k capital over 5 years x 2,000 h, i.e. $60/h, scaled to $240/h at a 25% duty cycle. A 2-hour scan therefore costs $480 machine time, plus about $1,000 analysis labour (about 8 h), for about $1,480 per specimen. A service bureau costs about $2,300 ($450/h + $1,000 labour + $400 shipping). Larger parts may cost 5-10x more to analyse. The EMI alternative is estimated at about $324 per specimen (about 90 min).
NRE_note: Not addressed.
Production_note: Not addressed.
QA_Qual_note: Not addressed.
QA_Insp_note: Explicit per-specimen CT cost build-up (capital depreciation, duty cycle, labour, outsourcing) compared with EMI.
Storage_note: Not addressed.
Shared_Capital_note: Shows how CT capital cost per scan depends on utilization (duty cycle) — capital spreading for inspection equipment; no multi-user analysis.
Shared_Capacity_note: Not addressed.
Speed_note: Not addressed.

name: Multivariate equivalency testing framework for AM requalification (Lynch et al., UTEP) with R package MultivariateEquivalency
developer: University of Texas at El Paso W.M. Keck Center and collaborators (Lynch, Villalobos, Valadez Mesta, Gomez Guillen, Mireles, Wicker)
description: Feature-wise equivalence tests on percentile bins of the reference process, with family-wise error control across measured attributes. Simulations map trade-offs among power, detectable effect size, feature count and fabrication/measurement cost. Validation used 40 observations per process and three geometric features. The authors position it as a requalification screen, not a replacement for formal qualification.
NRE_note: Not addressed.
Production_note: Not addressed.
QA_Qual_note: Supports equivalence-based requalification and reports sample-size/cost trade-offs in simulation; specific cost figures not seen (abstract only).
QA_Insp_note: Not addressed.
Storage_note: Not addressed.
Shared_Capital_note: Equivalence screening lets a qualified baseline be extended to new machines; qualitative in the abstract.
Shared_Capacity_note: Not addressed.
Speed_note: Not addressed.

name: NAVAIR Additive Manufacturing Capability initiative: licensed Material Process Combination (MPC) qualification data packages (Colibrium Additive contract) and FRCE depot certification
year: 2026 (FRCE first certified metal AM parts reported April 2026; Colibrium MPC award reported May 2026)
developer: Naval Air Systems Command (NAVAIR AM Team) with Colibrium Additive (GE Aerospace); Fleet Readiness Center East (FRCE) depot
description: NAVAIR licenses six alloy Material Process Combinations. Each includes characterization data and curves, optimized parameters, consolidated material and process specifications, and design allowables for the tested properties, plus thin-wall fatigue characterization and workforce training. FRCE, working with the NAVAIR AM Team and Fleet Support Teams, qualified, produced and certified its first metal AM parts in under six months, which it called the fastest such effort in NAVAIR. The parts were an AH-1Z pylon fitting, a V-22 landing-gear door stop fitting and a C-130 blanking plate, in aluminum, described as non-flight-critical. No contract value, cost or tiered criteria are public.
NRE_note: Supplies optimized process parameters and specifications that remove part of the NRE; not costed.
Production_note: Only trade press and a Navy news story describe the program; neither mentions cost, so whether production cost is treated is not established.
QA_Qual_note: Pre-qualified MPC data and allowables shorten qualification (FRCE: under 6 months), but there is no tiered framework or cost data.
QA_Insp_note: The public stories say only that parts meet the same quality requirements as conventional parts, so per-part inspection is not described.
Storage_note: The stories describe in-house, on-demand production but say nothing about inventory, so whether storage is treated is not established.
Shared_Capital_note: Reuse of one licensed MPC package across NAVAIR parts and sites was the earlier researcher's inference; the sources do not state it.
Shared_Capacity_note: The Navy story mentions FRCE, Lakehurst and Fleet Support Teams but not sharing machines or capacity, so this is not established.
Speed_note: Aims to cut lead times and aircraft downtime; only the qualification-time figure (under 6 months) is quantified.

name: EDA Additive Manufacturing Feasibility Study & Technology Demonstration (EDA-AM, deployable AM factory)
developer: European Defence Agency (contract EDA-16.ESI.OP.144); performed by Fundacion Prodintec and MBDA France
description: EDA-commissioned study mapping defence AM applications, value chains and limitations, with a State of the Art Report and a Strategic Report. A self-contained AM 'factory' module was deployed in an EDA-sponsored airlift exercise to gather data on AM in operations. No part selection method, business case or cost model is published.
NRE_note: Only a conference poster and press describe the study, and its reports are not public, so design or reverse-engineering effort cannot be confirmed either way.
Production_note: Only a poster and press describe the study; the poster expects 'substantial economic benefits' but the reports that might cost production are not public.
QA_Qual_note: Certification, standardisation, IPR and training named as the main non-technical limits; not quantified [1].
QA_Insp_note: Only a poster and press describe the study, and they do not say whether inspection is considered; the reports are not public.
Storage_note: Digital spare-part storage with on-demand production examined as an example application; not quantified [2].
Shared_Capital_note: Only a poster and press describe the study, and they do not say whether machine investment or sharing is assessed.
Shared_Capacity_note: Deployable self-contained AM module tested in an airlift exercise; no capacity or placement model [1].
Speed_note: Field repair and maintenance and a reduced logistic burden cited as expected benefits; not quantified [2].

name: DGA industrial orientation note on additive manufacturing (defence AM action plan incl. in-service support/MCO)
developer: Direction generale de l'armement (DGA), France; defence AM working group launched early 2023
description: Policy note stating that AM complements rather than replaces conventional manufacturing, and that design offices should use AM where useful but not for every part. Its action plan covers defining MCO use cases and business models, a common agile qualification process, large machines serving the whole defence industry, and sharing demand forecasts with subcontractors. No scoring or cost method is given.
NRE_note: Not addressed beyond advising design offices to use AM where useful [1].
Production_note: States conventional methods will in some cases remain more suitable and cost-effective; no cost method [1].
QA_Qual_note: Calls for an agile, robust, generalisable qualification process with industry and a shared normative standard; not costed [1].
QA_Insp_note: Not addressed; post-processing appears only as a value-chain step [1].
Storage_note: Spares not held in stock and on-demand production near the point of use cited as benefits; not quantified [1].
Shared_Capital_note: Large French machines being developed to serve the whole defence industry, and consolidation of small firms; qualitative [1].
Shared_Capacity_note: Proposes a multi-sector network and sharing demand forecasts with subcontractors; no mechanism or model [1].
Speed_note: Cites Ukraine as showing AM's value for spares in theatre; expects lower MCO costs and operational constraints; not quantified [1].

name: DGA OptiFab study: AM anti-blast protection and pre-qualified spare parts catalogue for light armoured vehicles
developer: DGA (with the Agence de l'innovation de defense) and ARQUUS; testing at DGA Techniques aeronautiques, Toulouse
decision_levels: Part selection; Process/machine choice; Capacity placement/sharing
description: DGA study that compares several manufacturing methods to pick the best for anti-blast parts. It also tests whether light-vehicle spares could be made additively in maintenance workshops. 'Cloned' AM parts are characterised against the originals, first on the bench and then on vehicles, toward a catalogue of pre-qualified spare parts.
NRE_note: Parts are 'cloned' (reproduced from originals); effort not costed [1].
Production_note: Only trade press describes the study; it gives no cost figures and does not show whether production cost is assessed.
QA_Qual_note: Cloned AM parts characterised against originals, then bench and vehicle tests, toward a pre-qualified catalogue; burden not quantified [1].
QA_Insp_note: Only trade press describes the study; it covers bench and vehicle characterisation but does not say whether per-part inspection is considered.
Storage_note: Reducing stockpiles named as a goal; not quantified [1].
Shared_Capital_note: Only trade press describes the study, and it does not say whether machine investment or sharing is assessed.
Shared_Capacity_note: Printers at certain bases, including overseas theatres; no counts or capacity model [1].
Speed_note: Parts made when needed without waiting for resupply; not quantified [1].

name: ROK procedure for applying 3D-printed repair parts in operational units (DMSMS / FMECA / localisation screening with DT&E-OT&E qualification)
developer: S. Yoo (ROK Ministry of National Defense), J. Hur (ROK Naval Academy), H. Lee (ROK Navy Force Support System Project Group)
description: Qualitative screening built on existing parts-localisation procedures. Candidates come from three pools: DMSMS-tracked obsolete parts, FMECA risk level 2-3 parts with poor MTBF/MKBF/MRBF, and foreign-sourced parts with high import-substitution value. Each passes DT&E, an installation test, OT&E and a military-suitability determination before being catalogued in a parts database. The programme (since 2017) was extended by a 2025 industry-defence ministry agreement.
NRE_note: The full paper mentions reverse modelling only as a software capability and does not treat design or reverse-engineering effort in its screening or qualification steps.
Production_note: Manufacturing ease and cost considered qualitatively for the localisation pool; cites an F-15K HPT cover plate at 90% lower purchase cost; no model [1].
QA_Qual_note: Staged DT&E, installation test, OT&E and military-suitability determination specified; burden not quantified [1].
QA_Insp_note: Refers to national quality guidelines covering equipment, materials, printed outputs and software; no per-part inspection cost [1].
Storage_note: Inventory effects not analysed [1].
Shared_Capital_note: The full paper calls for expanding military printing facilities and a national defence centre but does not address sharing machine investment.
Shared_Capacity_note: The full paper does not analyse sharing printing capacity between units or services.
Speed_note: FMECA/MTBF screening targets parts whose failures cut mission capability; cites procurement shortened by >30 days; not valued [1].

name: Satair/Airbus AM spare-part pre-assessment and RapidSpares recertification route
year: 2015-2020 (AM team since c. 2015; first certified metal flying spare 2020)
developer: Satair (Airbus aftermarket subsidiary) AM team with Airbus RapidSpares design offices; production at Airbus Filton Reference Manufacturing shop
description: When a part becomes non-procurable or an AOG order arrives, Satair's AM team runs a short pre-assessment and hands candidates to Airbus RapidSpares design offices for redesign and recertification. In the A320ceo wingtip fence case, AM beat both re-tooling the casting and redesigning for machining. Satair reports more than 300 AM-certified part numbers.
NRE_note: Non-recurring cost compared across alternatives: mould replacement and machining redesign rejected, AM NRC 45% lower in one case. Method not published [1][2].
Production_note: A four-part shipset per 26 h build lowers cost per piece; no per-part cost model [1][2].
QA_Qual_note: Former cast part recertified in ~5 weeks via a new certification process; ships with EASA Form 1; shop process-qualified 2019. A case outcome, not a modelled burden [1][2].
QA_Insp_note: Only press releases describe the route; they mention post-processing but not inspection.
Storage_note: Only press releases describe the route, and they do not discuss inventory.
Shared_Capital_note: Only press releases describe the route, and they do not say whether machine investment is considered.
Shared_Capacity_note: Only press releases describe the route; they name the Filton print shop but say nothing about shared capacity.
Speed_note: AOG-triggered; total lead time reduced (no figure); a 2015 Qantas polymer part was prototyped within days; not valued [1][3].

name: ST Engineering AM parts screening, business case and certification workflow (with EOS Additive Minds)
developer: ST Engineering Aerospace (Advanced Manufacturing Design Centre, Singapore), with an EOS Additive Minds capability transfer
description: A late-2018 capability-transfer programme gave ST Engineering a process for parts screening and selection, DfAM, business case analysis and critical-to-quality requirements. ST then built its own workflow covering DfAM, powder management, printing, inspection and post-processing. Parts are printed on demand from certified files under EASA/FAA/CAAS approvals, and more than 120 part numbers are in a production digital catalogue.
NRE_note: DfAM and assembly consolidation are part of the method; not costed [1].
Production_note: Business case analysis is a method step; no figures or model published [1][3].
QA_Qual_note: Qualification campaign to B-basis design values, proof-load tests, EASA STC/DOA/POA; burden not modelled in selection [1].
QA_Insp_note: Inspection is a workflow step and all parts undergo QA with traceability; not costed [1][3].
Storage_note: Virtual inventory; on-demand printing reduces non-moving inventory; not quantified [1].
Shared_Capital_note: Only a vendor case study and company brochures describe the method; it has a business-case step, but its contents, including machine investment, are not public.
Shared_Capacity_note: Certified files printed on qualified printers close to aircraft sites; no capacity model [1].
Speed_note: Shorter turnaround and 'drastically shorter lead time' claimed; no figures [1][3].

name: Leonardo Aircraft Division AM spare-part candidate criteria (safety, feasibility, lead time >180 days, unscheduled removal rate band)
developer: Leonardo S.p.A. Aircraft Division Customer Support (Caselle, Turin) with Politecnico di Torino (A. Pochettino MSc thesis; builds at IAM@PoliTo)
description: Four screening criteria: non-safety-critical (binary); feasibility (geometry, material, volume, cost); procurement lead time over 180 days; and unscheduled removal rate of 0.050-0.500 per 1,000 flight hours. They yielded three use cases: a C-27J main landing gear bracket, an M-346 clevis and an M-345 connector. Leonardo reports more than 100 metal AM parts qualified and flying. This is separate from the earlier pass's Viano business-model entry for the same division.
NRE_note: CAD rebuilt from drawings and material substitution (Al 2024 to AlSi10Mg) discussed; effort not costed [1].
Production_note: Feasibility requires AM to be cost-effective at small to medium volumes; per-part AM costs for the three chosen parts (about EUR 69-105, from the AMOtool app) are estimated after selection, not within the screen.
QA_Qual_note: Safety-critical parts excluded; relies on Leonardo's existing certification path (AlSi10Mg certified); not quantified [1].
QA_Insp_note: Each order built in two copies, the second tested as first article (dimensional, chemical-physical, mechanical); not costed [1].
Storage_note: On-demand production to simplify warehouse management; not quantified [1].
Shared_Capital_note: The thesis lists the four criteria but says the full selection process is out of its scope, and its later chapters could not be extracted, so machine investment or sharing cannot be ruled out.
Shared_Capacity_note: The thesis says the full selection process is out of its scope and its later chapters could not be extracted, so whether capacity is considered is unconfirmed.
Speed_note: Quantified screening thresholds on lead time (>180 days) and removal rate, plus AOCP status; value of availability not modelled [1].

name: EPRI Quick Insight Brief: Additive Manufacturing to Support Spare and Replacement Items (3002019767)
developer: Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI)
decision_levels: Part selection; Adopt or make-vs-buy; Capacity placement/sharing
description: Short brief listing considerations for using AM for replacement items. They are process limits, QA scope (reverse-engineering measurements, CAD/CAM, fabrication), material equivalency for safety-related items, software control and counterfeiting. It gives utility examples and plans a member capability inventory, an application library and best-practice guidance.
NRE_note: QA must cover reverse-engineering measurements and CAD/CAM data creation; cost not separated [1].
Production_note: Example: AM connector ~$150 each with no minimum vs ~$120,000 OEM order with a 100-piece minimum per type; no cost model [1].
QA_Qual_note: Material equivalency must be established for safety-related items; best-practice guidance planned in 12-18 months [1].
QA_Insp_note: Verifying that items meet design named as a challenge; no inspection methods [1].
Storage_note: Avoiding minimum order quantities and managing obsolescence noted; no stocking guidance [1].
Shared_Capital_note: The brief notes the 'potential to share resources such as additive manufacturing and laser light measurement machines' among members and that one utility used an outside shop; no investment figures are given.
Shared_Capacity_note: Planned inventory of member and supplier AM capabilities that could lead to regional centres for spares [1].
Speed_note: Lead-time examples: OEM 46 weeks vs ~3 weeks AM; 3-month quote vs <1 week; not valued [1].

name: EDF case-by-case AM of obsolete nuclear auxiliary-circuit parts and EDF Hydro WAAM programme
developer: EDF (R&D, nuclear fleet and EDF Hydro) with partners incl. CIH, Institut de Soudure and INOVSYS
description: EDF selects obsolete parts case by case and limits nuclear use to auxiliary circuits, not the primary circuit. Worn parts are 3D-scanned and rebuilt, either printed directly (a valve plug by SLM) or cast from a printed mould. The process is chosen by part size and use (SLM, cold spray or WAAM). EDF says it has not yet entered an industrial phase.
NRE_note: 3D scanning and rebuilding of worn parts described; not costed [1].
Production_note: Design and material optimisation said to reduce cost; no figures [1].
QA_Qual_note: RCC-M does not yet cover AM, and EDF aims to add it within three years; parts must match conventional mechanical performance [1].
QA_Insp_note: Adapting NDT (magnetic particle, ultrasonic, eddy current) to AM named as a main open question; not costed [1].
Storage_note: Only an EDF web interview describes the approach, and it does not discuss inventory.
Shared_Capital_note: Only an EDF web interview describes the approach, and it does not say whether machine investment or sharing is considered.
Shared_Capacity_note: Only an EDF web interview describes the approach; partners are named but their capacity is not discussed.
Speed_note: EDF Hydro aims to cut unit unavailability costs significantly, and cold spray shortens tube repairs; not quantified [1].

name: Siemens Energy (Siemens Industrial Turbomachinery) Finspang AM burner repair and spares programme
developer: Siemens Industrial Turbomachinery AB, Finspang (now Siemens Energy); Materials Solutions, Worcester (acquired 2016)
description: Problem-driven adoption: eroded burner tips are repaired by machining off the worn section and reprinting it, instead of buying new burners. A digital thread (NX, Teamcenter, MOM tracking powder reuse) supports the work. No formal part screening or business-case method is published.
NRE_note: Redesign without casting moulds or costly iterations, and a 13-to-1 burner-head consolidation, described; not costed [1].
Production_note: Repair said to be more cost-effective than a new burner; ~50% material saving; no model [1][2].
QA_Qual_note: Repaired burners recertified; field evidence from inspection after 20,000 operating hours; not modelled [1].
QA_Insp_note: Automated 3D scanning and in-line/off-line monitoring planned; not costed [1].
Storage_note: On-demand printing of spares presented as a future goal; not quantified [1].
Shared_Capital_note: Trade press reports large investment in an eight-machine AM facility but does not say whether investment or sharing enters any part decision.
Shared_Capacity_note: Siemens AM Network links designers and service providers; not modelled [1].
Speed_note: Burner repair turnaround cut 70% (an outcome, not decision-model output) [1].

name: GE annual part audit and per-part ROI screen for casting-to-AM conversion (LM9000 bleed air adapter caps)
developer: GE Aviation (now GE Aerospace) with GE Additive; parts for Baker Hughes LM9000 turbines
description: In GE's 2020 annual part audit, the team reviewed hundreds of purchased castings, found 180 suitable for AM, and calculated ROI for each. It chose four CoCr bleed air adapter caps as the most profitable and checked them against quotes from four outside vendors. Reported results: ~35% lower manufacturing cost and 10 months from identification to prototypes.
NRE_note: Only minor print tweaks needed, and existing casting moulds were a factor; NRE not reported as a separate term [1].
Production_note: Per-part ROI calculated for 180 candidates; AM cost compared with vendor casting quotes (~35% lower) [1].
QA_Qual_note: Printed parts matched cast quality within weeks; no formal qualification process described [1].
QA_Insp_note: Only one trade-press article describes the audit, and it does not say whether inspection cost enters the ROI.
Storage_note: Only one trade-press article describes the audit; it mentions reduced spare-sourcing risk but not whether inventory is assessed.
Shared_Capital_note: Only one trade-press article describes the audit, and it does not say whether machine investment is in the ROI.
Shared_Capacity_note: Only one trade-press article describes the audit, and it does not mention capacity.
Speed_note: Time to market a stated criterion: 10 months vs a typical 12-18 for castings; spare-sourcing risk reduced; not valued [1].

name: Anglo American spare parts inventory analysis and local on-demand AM pilot (with CSIR and Ivaldi)
developer: Anglo American with South Africa's CSIR and Ivaldi Group
description: Two-step project: analyse Anglo American's spare parts inventory and the impact of a digitally distributed supply chain, then digitise, produce locally and test selected parts at South African operations. No screening criteria or metrics are published.
NRE_note: Parts to be digitised; effort not costed [1].
Production_note: Only a press release and a trade article describe the project; they mention savings but do not show whether production cost is assessed.
QA_Qual_note: Local testing of produced parts planned; no criteria [1][2].
QA_Insp_note: Only a press release and a trade article describe the project, and they do not say whether inspection is considered.
Storage_note: Sending 'files, not physical spare parts' to cut logistics costs; not quantified [1].
Shared_Capital_note: Only a press release and a trade article describe the project, and they do not say whether machine investment or sharing is assessed.
Shared_Capacity_note: On-demand production by local manufacturers near operations; no capacity model [1][2].
Speed_note: Shorter delivery lead times claimed; not quantified [1].

name: Sandvik-Boliden on-demand printed drill-rig spare parts trial
developer: Sandvik Mining and Rock Solutions with Boliden
description: Proof-of-concept trial installing redesigned metal-printed parts on Boliden drill rigs to test local on-demand supply. The parts are bushes, brackets and drill parts replaced every 3,000-4,000 h. Costs, IP, warranty and liability are listed as open questions.
NRE_note: Components 'specially redesigned' for AM; not costed [1].
Production_note: Only trade press describes the trial; it says cost is still an open question, so whether it will be assessed is not known.
QA_Qual_note: Field performance evaluation at proof-of-concept stage; warranty and liability unresolved [1].
QA_Insp_note: Only trade press describes the trial, and it does not mention inspection.
Storage_note: Aims to avoid tying up capital in stock for many part numbers; not quantified [1].
Shared_Capital_note: Only trade press describes the trial, and it does not say whether machine investment is assessed.
Shared_Capacity_note: Local printing for customers raised; current production at one Sandvik facility; who prints remains open [1].
Speed_note: Faster delivery cited; not quantified [1].
